inputs.question_text: How does blue-green deployment reduce downtime during releases?
inputs.answer_text: Blue-green deployment works by keeping two identical production environments, 'blue' (currently live) and 'green' (the new version). You deploy the new release to the idle environment and run health checks and smoke tests against it while the blue environment keeps serving all real traffic, so users are never exposed to an in-progress deployment. Once the green environment passes its checks, you switch the router or load balancer to send traffic to green instead of blue -- ideally an atomic, near-instant cutover rather than a gradual rollout -- so there's no window where some requests hit a half-updated environment. If something goes wrong after the cutover, you roll back by simply switching the router back to blue, which is still fully intact and warm, giving you a much faster and safer rollback path than trying to redeploy the previous version.

inputs.question_text: How does cache invalidation get handled in your caching layer?
inputs.answer_text: There are a few standard strategies for cache invalidation. TTL-based expiration is the simplest: every cached entry gets a time-to-live, and once it expires the next read falls through to the database and repopulates the cache -- simple, but it means the cache can serve stale data for up to the TTL window after an underlying write. Write-through caching avoids that staleness by updating the cache synchronously whenever the underlying data changes, at the cost of extra latency on every write. Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the most common pattern: the application checks the cache first, and on a miss it loads from the database and populates the cache; invalidation then means explicitly deleting or updating the cached key whenever the underlying record changes, which keeps reads fast but pushes correctness onto the application code doing the invalidation correctly and consistently.

inputs.question_text: Why do distributed consensus systems use randomized election timeouts?
inputs.answer_text: In Raft-style consensus, every follower waits for a heartbeat from the current leader within an election timeout window, and starts a new election if it doesn't hear one in time. If every node used the exact same fixed timeout, they'd all time out simultaneously whenever a leader fails, and every one of them would start a new election at once -- splitting the vote so no candidate gets a majority, which forces another round and can repeat indefinitely. Randomizing each node's timeout within a range means one node almost always times out first, becomes a candidate, and gathers votes from the still-waiting followers before their own timers expire, so split votes become rare and the cluster converges on a new leader quickly.

inputs.question_text: What does at-least-once delivery mean for the Background Job Queue, and how did you handle it?
inputs.answer_text: At-least-once delivery means a consumer might see the same message more than once, so the work has to be idempotent. project.title: Sharded Counter
project.summary: A high-write counter split across shards.

inputs.question_text: Walk me through how the counter avoids write contention.
inputs.answer_text: A single counter key would be a hot spot with everyone incrementing it. So I split it into several shard keys and each increment picks a shard at random, spreading the writes. To read the total I sum all the shards. It trades a slightly more expensive read for much cheaper concurrent writes. The number of shards is the knob, more shards means less contention but a costlier read.

project.title: Consistent Hashing
project.summary: Distributing keys across cache nodes.

inputs.question_text: Can you explain why consistent hashing is used to spread keys across cache nodes?
inputs.answer_text: Plain modulo hashing over the node count means that adding or removing a node changes almost every key's assignment, so nearly the whole cache has to move, a huge disruption. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring, and a key belongs to the next node clockwise, so adding or removing a node only remaps the keys in that node's arc, a small fraction, leaving the rest untouched. Virtual nodes are added so each physical node covers several arcs, which smooths out hotspots and uneven distribution. So it is chosen specifically to minimize reshuffling when the cluster changes size.

project.title: Deadlock Incident
project.summary: Transactions deadlocking under load.

inputs.question_text: What broke to cause the deadlocks under concurrent updates?
inputs.answer_text: Under load, transactions started failing with deadlock errors. The cause was inconsistent lock ordering: one code path updated account A then B, another updated B then A, so two concurrent transactions could each hold one and wait for the other, a classic circular wait. The database detected it and killed one, hence the errors. The fix was to always acquire the rows in a consistent order, I sorted the ids before locking, so two transactions touching the same pair always grab them in the same sequence and cannot form a cycle. I also added a retry on deadlock as a safety net since they can still happen rarely. Reproducing it with two concurrent transactions in the opposite order is how I confirmed the cause. That was my fix.

project.title: Cache Stampede Fix
project.summary: Preventing a stampede when a hot key expires.

inputs.question_text: If a single hot cache key expiring caused a stampede, how would you prevent it?
inputs.answer_text: The problem is that when a hot key expires, every concurrent request misses at once and they all recompute the expensive value simultaneously, hammering the backend. A few complementary fixes: have only one request recompute by taking a short lock on the key while others briefly wait or serve stale, so the backend sees one recompute not thousands. Or stale-while-revalidate, serve the slightly expired value while one background refresh updates it, so no request ever blocks on a cold recompute. And jitter the TTLs so many keys do not all expire at the exact same second. I would use single-flight recompute plus jittered TTL, since together they cover both the hot-key and the mass-expiry cases. I implemented the single-flight lock on this project.

If a retry comes with the same key, the insert fails on the unique constraint, and instead of redoing the work I return the stored result from the first attempt. The concurrency subtlety is two retries arriving at the exact same time, both trying to insert, the unique constraint means only one wins the insert and does the work, the other has to wait and then read the result, so I handle the loser by having it poll or wait for the first to finish rather than proceeding. inputs.answer_text: Each row has a version number. When a client reads a record to edit it, they get the current version, and when they save, the update says set the new values and bump the version, but only where the version still equals the one they read. If nobody else changed it in between, the version matches, the update succeeds, and the version increments. If someone else saved first, the version has already moved, so the where clause matches zero rows, the update affects nothing, and I detect that and tell the client their copy is stale rather than blindly overwriting the other person's change. The client then re-reads and reapplies. It is optimistic because it assumes conflicts are rare and only pays a cost when one actually happens, versus locking the row up front. project.title: At-Least-Once Pipeline
project.summary: A pipeline that must not lose events even on failures.

inputs.question_text: If the pipeline must never lose an event even when a consumer crashes, how would you guarantee that?
inputs.answer_text: The key is the order of operations around the offset commit. The consumer must fully process an event, and only after the downstream write succeeds does it commit the offset for that event. If it crashes before committing, on restart it re-reads from the last committed offset and reprocesses, so nothing is lost, that is at-least-once. The cost is that a crash after processing but before committing means the event gets processed twice on restart, so the downstream has to be idempotent, keyed on the event id, or you get duplicates. So the guarantee is: process then commit, never commit then process, plus idempotent downstream to make the inevitable reprocessing safe. Committing offsets before processing would be at-most-once and could lose events, which is exactly what we must avoid here. I would build it that way.

project.title: Audit Logging
project.summary: An audit log of sensitive actions you built.

inputs.question_text: If the audit log had to be trustworthy for a security investigation, how would you design it?
inputs.answer_text: For an audit log to be trustworthy two things matter: it has to capture everything relevant, and it has to be hard to tamper with, because an attacker who can edit the log can erase their tracks. For completeness I would log at a choke point every sensitive action passes through, like the authorization layer, rather than relying on each feature to remember to log, so nothing is silently missed. For integrity I would make it append-only, no update or delete permissions on the log table even for the app's own role, and ideally write to a separate store with restricted access so compromising the app does not grant log-editing. To detect tampering I would chain records with a hash of the previous entry so any deletion or edit breaks the chain and is detectable. I would also log the actor, action, target, timestamp, and outcome, since a log missing who or what is useless in an investigation. So: capture at a choke point, append-only with restricted access, and hash-chaining for tamper-evidence. I built the append-only capture; the hash-chaining is what I would add to harden it.

inputs.question_text: Walk me through the incident where some customers got charged twice.
inputs.answer_text: A small number of customers were double-charged, which is about the worst bug for trust. The pattern was that it happened on requests that were slow, and the cause was a client-side retry meeting a non-idempotent charge endpoint: when the first charge request was slow, the client timed out and retried, but the first one had actually succeeded on the server, so the retry created a second charge. The server had no way to recognize the retry as the same intended charge. Immediate response was to identify the affected customers by finding duplicate charges with near-identical timestamps and refund them, and communicate. The real fix was idempotency keys, the client sends a unique key per charge intent, the server records it, and a retry with the same key returns the original result instead of charging again, enforced with a unique constraint so even concurrent retries cannot both charge. I also tightened timeouts so the mismatch window shrank. I led the diagnosis, the refund backfill, and the idempotency fix. The lesson was that any retried money operation must be idempotent, full stop.

project.title: Vector Clocks
project.summary: Ordering events across distributed nodes.

inputs.question_text: Can you explain what a vector clock captures that a plain timestamp does not?
inputs.answer_text: A plain wall-clock timestamp only tells you when an event happened on that node's own clock, and clocks across nodes drift, so comparing timestamps across nodes does not reliably tell you which event actually happened first, and it certainly cannot tell you whether two events were causally related or just coincidentally concurrent. A vector clock instead tracks, per node, a counter for every node it knows about, incrementing its own on each event and merging in the max of any counters it observes from messages. Comparing two vector clocks tells you whether one causally happened-before the other, or whether neither did, meaning they were genuinely concurrent, which a timestamp alone cannot distinguish. project.title: Gradient Descent
project.summary: How gradient descent updates model weights.

inputs.question_text: Can you explain how gradient descent updates the model's weights during training?
inputs.answer_text: During the forward pass, the model produces a prediction and the loss function measures how far that prediction is from the true label. Backpropagation then computes the gradient of that loss with respect to every weight in the network, which tells you the direction each weight would need to move to increase the loss. Gradient descent updates each weight by moving it a small step in the opposite direction of its gradient, since moving opposite the gradient decreases the loss, and the size of that step is scaled by the learning rate. Too large a learning rate can overshoot and fail to converge, while too small makes training painfully slow, so it's usually tuned rather than left at an arbitrary default.

project.title: Outbox Pattern for Reliable Events
project.summary: Ensuring a database write and a published event never disagree.

inputs.question_text: Walk me through how you made sure the database write and the published event couldn't disagree with each other.
inputs.answer_text: The naive approach was to write to the database and then publish an event right after in the same request, but that has a gap: if the database write succeeds and the process crashes before the publish, or the publish itself fails, the event is silently lost even though the database committed, so downstream systems never learn about a change that genuinely happened. I used the outbox pattern instead: within the same database transaction as the actual write, I also insert a row representing the event into an outbox table, so either both the write and the outbox row commit together or neither does. A separate background process reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka, retrying on failure, and marks them published only after a successful publish. That guarantees the event eventually gets published if and only if the underlying write actually committed, at the cost of publish latency being slightly delayed rather than instantaneous, and needing to be careful the publisher's retries don't cause the same event to be published twice, which downstream consumers need to handle idempotently. I designed and built the outbox table and the publisher process.

project.title: MVCC
project.summary: How multi-version concurrency control lets readers and writers avoid blocking each other.

inputs.question_text: Can you explain how MVCC lets a reader see consistent data without blocking a concurrent writer?
inputs.answer_text: Instead of a writer locking a row and forcing readers to wait, MVCC keeps multiple versions of a row, and when a transaction writes, it creates a new version rather than overwriting the old one in place. A reader's transaction is given a consistent snapshot of the database as of when it started, so it keeps seeing the version of each row that existed at that snapshot time, even if another transaction commits a new version of that row afterward, which is why the reader never needs to acquire a lock that would block on that writer. Old row versions eventually get cleaned up once no active transaction could still need to see them.

inputs.answer_text: A single consumer instance would fall further and further behind at ten times the volume, so I'd add more consumer instances pulling from the same queue in parallel, since RabbitMQ distributes messages across however many consumers are connected. inputs.question_text: Which trade-off did you accept using interrupts instead of polling for that sensor?

inputs.question_text: Why did you add a mechanism to prevent a stampede when a popular cache key expires?

project.title: Write-Ahead Log

inputs.question_text: Can you explain how a write-ahead log protects data if the database crashes mid-write?
inputs.answer_text: Before a change is applied to the actual data pages on disk, the database first writes a record of that change to the write-ahead log and makes sure that log record is durably on disk. If the database crashes after the log record is written but before the actual data page is updated, on restart the database replays the log from the last checkpoint forward, reapplying any committed changes that hadn't yet made it into the data pages, so no committed transaction is lost even though the crash happened mid-write. project.title: Blue-Green Deployment

inputs.question_text: Why did you set up blue-green deployment instead of a rolling deploy for that service?
inputs.answer_text: With a rolling deploy, if a bad release starts causing errors, some fraction of instances are already running the bad version and it takes time to roll each one back individually, during which users keep hitting the broken version on whichever instances haven't been rolled back yet. Blue-green keeps a full second environment on the previous version standing by, so if the newly deployed environment shows a problem, traffic can be switched back to the old environment for every instance at once, essentially instantly, rather than working through a rollback instance by instance. The cost is running two full environments during a deploy, which is more expensive than a rolling deploy that reuses the same instances, but for this particular service the ability to fully bail out instantly mattered more than the extra infrastructure cost during the deploy window.

project.title: Regularization
project.summary: How L2 regularization helps prevent overfitting.

inputs.question_text: Can you explain how L2 regularization helps with overfitting?
inputs.answer_text: L2 regularization adds a penalty term to the loss function proportional to the sum of the squares of the model's weights, so during training the model isn't just rewarded for fitting the training data well, it's also penalized for having unnecessarily large weight values. This discourages the model from relying too heavily on any single feature or fitting the training data's noise too precisely, since doing so would require large weights that now come with a cost. The result tends to be a smoother, less complex decision boundary that generalizes better to unseen data, at the cost of potentially underfitting if the regularization strength is set too high.

inputs.question_text: Walk me through how the service handles requests that are in flight when it needs to shut down.

I set the timeout based on our slowest typical request plus a margin, and if a request is still running past that timeout, it does get forcibly cut off, since waiting indefinitely for one stuck request would block the whole shutdown.

inputs.question_text: Which trade-off did you accept using an asynchronous event between those two services instead of a direct synchronous call?
inputs.answer_text: A synchronous call would mean the calling service is blocked waiting on the other service's response, and if that other service is slow or down, the caller is directly affected too, effectively coupling the two services' availability together. Publishing an event asynchronously instead means the calling service doesn't wait on the other service at all, it just publishes and moves on, and the other service processes it whenever it's able to, which decouples their availability from each other. The trade-off is that the calling service can no longer assume the effect has already happened by the time its own call returns, since the event might not be processed for a moment, so anything that genuinely needs an immediate, confirmed result has to use a synchronous call instead, this pattern only fit here because nothing downstream needed to respond to that specific outcome immediately.

inputs.question_text: Design a URL shortener service that needs to handle high read traffic. Walk me through your approach.
inputs.answer_text: Writes are cheap and rare compared to reads, so I'd optimize hard for read latency. Short codes get generated from a base62-encoded counter rather than hashing the URL, which avoids collision handling entirely and keeps codes short. Redirects themselves return a 301 so browsers cache them client-side too, cutting repeat traffic to the service further. I'd shard the counter or use a coordination-free ID scheme like Snowflake IDs if a single counter became a write bottleneck.
